title: SIGNAL GHOST
briefing: For three days, a transmitter on Channel A has appeared and vanished along the Port Merrin waterfront. Three receivers heard it at different places and times. Establish what is actually transmitting, and where. Everything here is fictional.

variants.label: Clear day
variants.summary: Clear, stable air. Propagation is short-range.

variants.label: Fog, morning
variants.summary: Fog with a temperature inversion. Signals can travel unusually far along the coast.

variants.label: After rain, evening
variants.summary: Cooling air over warm water after rain. Ducting is possible over the harbour.

hypotheses.claim: A single mobile transmitter is moving along the waterfront.
Two fixed transmitters, one at the harbour and one on the headland, are alternating.
A single fixed transmitter at the harbour light is audible only when atmospheric conditions allow.

sources.label: Merrin Ferry Operations
sources.limits: Authoritative for the ferry only. Says nothing about radio.

sources.label: Ferry position tracker
sources.limits: Tracks the ferry only, not other vessels.

sources.label: Harbour Authority
sources.limits: Interference log is compiled from the Quay receiver feed, not independent measurement.

sources.label: Spectrum licence registry
sources.limits: Last updated in 2023. Known to lag field changes.

sources.label: Port Merrin weather station
sources.limits: Point readings at the quay. Conditions on the headland may differ.

sources.label: Municipal monitoring station
sources.limits: Reports are summaries of the Quay receiver feed.

sources.label: Carrier fingerprint analysis
sources.limits: Shows the same hardware, not the same place.

sources.label: Calder Head receiver
sources.limits: Single omni antenna, no direction finding.

sources.label: Marlow Hotel receiver
sources.limits: Uncalibrated gain. Absolute levels are approximate.

sources.label: Ferry quay receiver
sources.limits: Single omni antenna, no direction finding.

sources.label: Harbour maintenance records
sources.limits: Records work done, not what the equipment transmits.

sources.label: Night angler, Calder Head
sources.limits: Saw a light, not a transmitter. Cannot say what it was.

sources.label: Ferry deckhand
sources.limits: Confident, but the watch he times events by runs fast.

evidence.title: Quay receiver: Channel A pulse train, day 1 07:10
evidence.reading: Channel A pulse train at 07:10, 1.2 s pulses, -91 dBm. Nothing heard at the Calder Head or Hotel receivers.

evidence.title: Calder Head receiver: strong Channel A, day 2 07:40
evidence.reading: Channel A pulse train at 07:40, 1.2 s pulses, -62 dBm. Far stronger than anything the Quay receiver has logged.

fog_morning.note: In fog with an inversion, a fixed source 4.6 km away is expected to reach Calder Head at roughly this level. The strong reading no longer implies the source is close.

evidence.title: Hotel receiver: strong Channel A, day 3 19:10
evidence.reading: Channel A pulse train at 19:10, 1.2 s pulses, -65 dBm. Not heard at the Hotel receiver on day 1.

post_rain_evening.note: After rain, cooling air over warm water produces a duct over the harbour. A fixed source at the breakwater light is expected to be strong here this evening.

evidence.title: Quay receiver: Channel A pulse train, day 1 12:40
evidence.reading: Channel A pulse train at 12:40, 1.2 s pulses, -90 dBm. Essentially the same level as 07:10.

evidence.title: Calder Head receiver: nothing at 12:40, day 1
evidence.reading: No Channel A detection at 12:40. Noise floor -110 dBm.
evidence.limits: A no-match: the receiver found nothing. It could not hear anything this weak at that range in clear air.

evidence.title: Ferry operator timetable
evidence.reading: Departures from the ferry quay at 07:10, 12:40 and 18:05 daily.
evidence.limits: A timetable. It says nothing about radio.

outcomes.note: The Quay receiver feed shows the same pulse train at every :10 and :40 all day. Only two of the three ferry departures line up, and the 18:05 departure has no signal. The ferry correlation is coincidence.
The data needed to check the ferry correlation could not be retrieved.

evidence.title: Weather station log, days 1 to 3
evidence.reading: Day 1 clear and stable. Day 2 fog with an inversion layer, 06:00 to 09:30. Day 3 rain 14:00 to 16:00, then rapid cooling in the evening.

evidence.title: Municipal monitoring report: emitter near the ferry terminal
evidence.reading: Emitter active near the ferry terminal at 07:10 and 12:40, coinciding with ferry departures.
evidence.limits: A summary of the Quay receiver feed. It is not a second measurement.

evidence.title: Harbour Authority interference log
evidence.reading: Channel A interference logged at the ferry quay at 07:10 and 12:40, coinciding with ferry departures.
evidence.limits: Compiled from the Quay receiver feed. It is not independent of E01 and E04.

evidence.title: Spectrum registry: breakwater beacon decommissioned
evidence.reading: The breakwater light beacon is listed as decommissioned in 2023. No active licence on Channel A at that site.
evidence.limits: Registry last updated in 2023. Field changes since then would not appear.

evidence.title: Maintenance work order: unit replaced on the breakwater light
evidence.reading: Beacon timer unit on the breakwater light replaced 21 days ago. The new unit was never entered in the spectrum registry.
evidence.limits: Records the work done. It does not state what the unit transmits.

evidence.title: Ferry position track, days 1 to 3
evidence.reading: At 07:40 on day 2 the ferry was moored at the quay. At 19:10 on day 3 it was in service on the far side of the bay. It was never within 3 km of Calder Head when the headland receiver heard Channel A.
evidence.limits: Tracks the ferry only. Other vessels are not covered.

evidence.title: Carrier fingerprint comparison, E01 / E02 / E03
evidence.reading: Carrier offset +2.1 kHz and pulse shape match across the Quay, Calder Head and Hotel captures to within 20 Hz. This is the same hardware.
evidence.limits: Shows the same hardware, not the same location.

evidence.title: Quay receiver: same pulse, day 2 07:40
evidence.reading: Channel A pulse train at 07:40, -91 dBm. This is the same pulse the Calder Head receiver logged at -62 dBm. The Quay level is unchanged from day 1.

evidence.title: Ferry deckhand: "it starts the moment we cast off"
evidence.reading: Says the signal cuts in right as the ferry casts off, every day, and is convinced the ferry is carrying it.
evidence.limits: Confident, but his watch runs fast.

outcomes.note: His watch runs 14 minutes fast. With the correction, his "cast off" times line up with the signal on two of three days.
The deckhand's watch could not be checked.

evidence.title: Night angler: a moving light on the water
evidence.reading: Saw a light moving across the water off Calder Head at about the time his radio crackled.
evidence.limits: A light is not a transmitter. He could not say what it was.

outcomes.note: The light matches a small fishing boat's running lights. No transmitter was aboard.
No vessel record matches what the angler saw. That is weak evidence at most: small boats often go unrecorded.

decision_points.prompt: Triage: which three items to inspect first.
Whether to spend budget corroborating the ferry-schedule correlation.
Whether to compare the two "independent" captures that share a receiver.
How to weigh the confident witness report against the device records.
Which hypothesis to reject first, and when.
How to read a corroboration that returns no-match versus one that could not be evaluated.
Whether to commit now or spend remaining budget.

debrief.truth: A single fixed beacon on the breakwater light, recently replaced and never re-registered, transmits on a fixed 30-minute cycle. Fog and post-rain ducting carry it far past its normal range, so it appears at different receivers on different days.

misleading_clues.why: The ferry correlation is coincidence. The pulse repeats every half hour all day, and only some ferry departures line up.
These are summaries of the Quay receiver feed. Counting them alongside E01 and E04 counts the same data three times.
Strong readings at distant receivers look like a nearby source, but ducting makes a distant fixed source strong there.
The registry is stale. The maintenance record shows the beacon was replaced and never re-registered.
A moving light is not a moving transmitter.

debrief.pivotal_explanation: E14 shows the same pulse at the Quay receiver at the same unchanged level while Calder Head heard it at -62 dBm. A mobile source cannot do that, and a fixed source with ducting can.
